speechtext:
that Bill S-2 (from the Senate) an Act to implement conventions between Canada and the Kingdom of the Netherlands and Canada and Japan and agreements between Canada and
the People's Republic of China and Canada and the Republic of Malta for avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by thanking Hon. Members on all sides of the House for allowing us to introduce this technical, but very important Bill which must be introduced today if we are going to take advantage of the fiscal year which begins on January 1, 1987. Apparently a 30 days' notice is needed so if this Bill is passed today we will have the proper notice period.
The purpose of this Bill is to implement conventions between Canada and the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Canada and Japan and what are known as agreements, not conventions, between Canada and the People's Republic of China and the Republic of Malta for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax. Before discussing the details of the Bill, and I will try to be very brief, I would like to say a few words about the whole desirability of the role of tax treaties.
Tax treaties are useful in order to promote international trade and to facilitate international investment. In particular, the existence of a tax treaty enshrining the basis as well as the rate of the applicable taxes provides a general air of tax stability which can only be reassuring to investors and traders. In short, a treaty rate of tax cannot be increased unless the treaty itself is modified or terminated. That is the heart of it. Termination is a rare event while revision is a lengthy process requiring the concurrence of two Governments. In both cases, taxpayers will normally receive advance notice of the impending changes.
Tax treaties also reduce annoyance in the operation of the tax system by eliminating the necessity of paying tax to the source country, if there is no permanent establishment in that country, and by providing a mechanism to settle problems encountered by taxpayers. More important, tax treaties eliminate or alleviate double taxation in instances in which international transactions are involved that may give rise to the same income being taxable in the hands of the same person by more than one state.
For the purpose of eliminating double taxation the tax treaties establish two categories of rules. First, in the case of a number of items of income, an exclusive right to tax is conferred on only one of the contracting states. In this way, the other contracting state is prevented from taxing and double taxation is absolutely avoided. Second, for other items of

November 27, 1986
Income Tax Agreements, 1986
income, the right to tax is not an exclusive one. These provisions confer on the state of source or situs a full or limited right of tax, and the state of residence must allow relief so as to avoid double taxation.
As we all know, the major reform of Canada's income tax legislation in 1971 required Canada to expand its network of double taxation conventions with other countries. Since that time negotiations for the conclusion of new treaties, or the revision of existing ones, have been entered into with almost 60 countries. I will be naming an additional number of them this morning.
In this Bill the four tax conventions under review follow the general pattern of the conventions previously approved by Parliament. Thus this Bill does not break the pattern but is consistent with it. The number of tax treaties in force at present is 40. The coventions with Cameroon, Guyana, Kenya, the Soviet Union and Zambia approved by Parliament in 1984, 1985 and 1986 are expected to be ratified in the near future. After their ratification the number of conventions in force will reach 45.
I would like to indicate briefly the main elements of these tax treaties. The country of which the payer is a resident can withhold tax, but the rate is generally limited to 10 per cent or 15 per cent in the case of dividends, branch tax and interest and, in the case of royalties, to 10 per cent.
Under the Canada-Netherlands Double Taxation Convention, the rate of withholding tax on dividends is reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent if the recipient is a company, other than a partnership, which owns directly at least 25 per cent of the capital of the company paying the dividends. Elowever, the existing convention contains a provision allowing corporations which meet a number of specific conditions to rapatriate dividends without having to pay any withholding tax. That convention will continue to apply for qualified corporations until December 31, 1988. The exemption in the Netherlands for mortgage interest received from Canada will continue to apply until June 30, 1987.
Some of the other matters also dealt with in these tax treaties include the following: capital gains, pension annuities, teachers and double taxation relief. I would be happy to go into them if it is necessary.
On balance, the terms of the tax conventions provide equitable solutions to the various problems of double taxation existing between Canada and these countries. Each of these countries hopes to implement the bilateral tax convention as soon as possible. Consequently, I commend this Bill to the most favourable consideration of the House.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT

speechtext:
The House resumed from Wednesday, November 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hockin that Bill C-27, an Act to facilitate the continuation of the business of the Bank of
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
British Columbia, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on this Bill with some pleasure, pleasure because it is satisfying for us from the West to be able to perform a service for the western people by dealing with legislation to enable the Bank of B.C. to continue its operations. I rise also with some sadness that it is necessary to do this. It is a tragedy for the Canadian economy and particularly the western Canadian economy that it has been made necessary to deal with legislation of this kind.
I would like to remind Hon. Members that the Bill is entitled an Act to facilitate the continuation of the business of the Bank of British Columbia. This Bill is about making sure that the Bank of B.C. can continue to operate without the threat of closure. We are acting upon the request of the Board of Directors that we do this. This is a business transaction that has taken place between two banks in order to facilitate the continuing operation of one of them.
Yesterday I listened at some length to the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). I enjoyed his intervention very much. He spoke like a banker. It was plain to see that he had been in the banking business for some time. He was at ease with the subject. It was clear that he was preoccupied with the ledgers of the banks and particularly the transfer of the $200 million from the CDIC to this particular transaction. I wish he had been equally concerned with some of the transactions in which the Big Five are engaged. I wish he had been as concerned about the millions of dollars the Bank of Montreal has had to write off in Latin America. Perhaps he could explain to us sometime how much that cost consumers of the Canadian banking industry.
The Big Five banks took risks in Latin America and now they have to write off amounts which they are asking Canadian consumers to pay. What about the Big Five's investment in Dome Petroleum to the tune of billions of dollars? They have exposed themselves so much that Dome has them where it wants them. The banks are continually rescheduling their debts so that Dome can stay afloat and they have to agree with everything for which Dome asks.
I wish the Hon. Member had been just as concerned about the activities of the Big Five as he was about the $200 million from CDIC which he keeps calling taxapayers' money. It would have been more proper for him to say that it was a part of company accounts and transfers into the CDIC made to ensure that the banking industry could remain afloat.
Why is this sale of the Bank of British Columbia to the Hongkong Bank necessary? As a non-banker, I would like to suggest that no bank the size of the Bank of British Columbia can withstand pressure from other corporations over a long period of time without getting into trouble. I would like to refer Hon. Members to a series of articles that appeared in Western Report magazine in January of this year. The first such article appeared on January 27, to be exact, and was

November 27, 1986
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
entitled "Let the T-D deny it's trying to devour the West's winning bank". In the opening paragraphs, Mr. Ted Byfield said:
A curious paragraph apepared last week in a Vancouver Sun advertisement run by the Toronto-Dominion Bank. It informed Vancouverites that the Toronto-Dominion is "a bank for British Columbians." The T-D has a quarter of a million customers in B.C., said the ad. It is "a major investor in B.C.," and while "nation-wide" in its operations it's "a British Columbia bank too."
A similar advertisement appeared in The Calgary Herald, aimed at Albertans. No such ads appeared, so far as we can tell, anywhere else in Canada. The question, of course, is why. Why this sudden regional consciousness? Why this abrupt discovery by a purely Toronto-based institution of an intense identity with the aspirations of two western provinces?
There can be only one possible answer. The only bank that operates chiefly in these two provinces is the Bank of British Columbia. The ads must therefore be aimed at the Bank of B.C. Unlike its two hapless Alberta neighbours, the Canadian Commercial and the Northland, the Bank of B.C. has achieved in the last two years an astounding success. It has written down its real estate loans to realistic levels.
It has wiped out most of its sour foreign investments (something that Toronto's Big Five have not attempted and do not like to discuss). It has secured an enormous injection of new equity capital. It has registered a $7 million profit. It has steadily expanded the number of its depositors. It has western stockholders, western directors, and western management, and it stands ready to provide alternative financing for western business when our loan applications are referred by the Big Fives' branch managers to their bosses in Toronto. So what's wrong with it? In the view of orthodox Canadian banking, one thing alone. Its headquarters are at Burrard and Pender Streets in Vancouver. To be a "sound" Canadian bank it must be located within a block of King and Bay Streets in Toronto. It must, that is, belong to The Club.
The article goes on to describe what Mr. Byfield sees as a concerted attempt on the part of the Big Five, or certainly on the part of the TD, to siphon off or drain away the customers who have been the loyal customers of the Bank of British Columbia, and therefore, weaken its position in the banking industry in western Canada. He then also invited the Toronto-Dominion Bank to reply, which it did in a subsequent issue. But Mr. Byfield goes on to say, in the February 17 issue of the Alberta report, under the headline "Just a few figures the TD mysteriously didn't notice". He makes several very important points as follows:
1.	Between June 1983 and June 1985, Alberta bank deposits increased by $599 million. That is, Albertans loaned that money to the banks. During the same period total bank loans to Albertans dropped by $1.24 billion. This can only mean that there was an outflow from Alberta of $1.84 billion over the period. Odd that the T-D didn't notice this.
2.	Similarly between June 1982 and June 1984, deposits of B.C. residents increased by $1,347 billion while total reported bank loans in B.C. declined by $769 million, resulting in a capital outflow from B.C. via the banking system of $2.116 billion. During the subsequent 12 months to June 30, 1985, deposits continued to grow faster than loans resulting in another $ 170-million outflow via the banks.
3.	In contrast, during the period from June 1981 to June 1983, bank loans in Ontario grew by $14,918 billion while bank deposits rose by a mere $2,359 billion. This reveals a $12.559-billion inflow into Ontario via the banks. This, of course, was when the Ontario-supported National Energy Program struck Alberta.
The statistics reveal another noteworthy fact. As of June 30, 1985, almost three-quarters of the $15 billion in business loans booked in Alberta fell into the category of $5 million or more, meaning of course that they would require approval in Toronto.
It goes on to deal with one other very important point. It
says:
There is one other banking statistic that the T-D has (one suspects unwittingly) divulged. It operates, it says, 122 branches in Alberta and 101 in B.C. According to the Canadian Payments Association Directory, Volume 1 for 1984 the Toronto-Dominion Bank as of December 1983, had 134 branches in Alberta and 107 in B.C. In other words during that 24-month period the T-D has closed 18 branches in Alberta and B.C., almost one every six weeks, a cutback of about 7.5 per cent.
The same directory reveals that between December 31, 1983 and December 31, 1984, the T-D reduced its national branch network by 10 (from 983 to 973), six in Alberta, four in B.C. and none in Ontario. As the Wyoming cattleman said, "When things get tough in our industry, our bank keeps on loaning money to us 'cause our bank's got nobody else to loan money to". The T-D on the other hand can find all kinds of people to loan money to, but they aren't in Alberta and B.C.
Now that, Mr. Speaker, is one of the reasons why I suspect the Bank of British Columbia has been in some difficulty. There has been a cash outflow by way of deposits from British Columbia and Alberta into central Canada into the five majors. There has been a disproportionate unwillingness to carry on a loan activity in those provinces that would become comparable to the type of investments made by the people of those two provinces in the five majors. If there is that type of siphoning off of cash from the western provinces, and an attempt on the part of the TD, and possibly the others, but certainly on the part of the TD, to get a market share that normally would have gone to the Bank of British Columbia, we can understand why there has been some pressure on the Bank of British Columbia.
I mentioned yesterday that the other possible reason is the fall-out from the National Energy Program. It would be easy to blame everything, all of our ills and woes on the National Energy Program. While much of it can be, it may be unfair to do all of it. I think we can conclude this. As I mentioned yesterday, we now know that about $60 billion flowed out of Alberta alone by way of the National Energy Program into eastern Canada, $60 billion that otherwise would have stayed there and would have been used in some other way than through the national tax scheme. That $60 billion means a lot to the western economy. Is it not possible, Mr. Speaker, that the Bank of British Columbia, in all good faith during the good years, lent $5 million, $10 million or $15 million to a small business in Alberta or British Columbia on the assumption that the economy was doing well, it would continue to do well, and that the cash flow would continue? Then, with the introduction of that Draconian tax program, bit by bit the $60 billion flowed out of the western economy.

The businesses were shocked by that siphoning off of funds from the economy and could no longer continue because of excessive taxation. They became overly exposed and had to declare bankruptcy. The Bank of British Columbia had to recognize that many of its loans were bad loans. It was not necessarily because of bad management; some of them may have been. It was because of a dramatic shift in the economy which nobody in the banking industry could have predicted.
November 27, 1986

There are just not the reserves in an institution the size of the Bank of British Columbia to withstand that kind of shock.
It is tragic that we have to deal with this legislation. It should never have happened. However, since we must do so, I am pleased the Government is in a position to help the economy of British Columbia and to help the B.C. banking industry remain solvent. The good news is that we will now have a bank in place in British Columbia which will have the security to withstand the kind of shock the Bank of British Columbia had to face and was unable to withstand. The Bank of Hongkong with its reserves will not be easily shaken by the kind of treatment the Bank of British Columbia had to endure.
There are some other advantages. B.C. is looking forward to taking part in western and Pacific Rim expansion. All of us recognize that much business is legitimately carried on through networking. The Big Five in Toronto know personally members of the corporations with whom they do business. They pick up the telephone and make agreements. It is not because they are avoiding any traditional business-like way of doing things, but because they know each other. We call it networking. That is one of the big pluses in having the Bank of Hongkong involved in a very substantial way in the banking industry in B.C. It opens up a whole new world of networking in the Pacific Rim. That is something which is possible now and was not possible hitherto. These people know each other. There is every reason to believe that people involved in the Bank of Hongkong know who are the movers and shakers in the Pacific Rim industry. They are willing to work with them. They can talk to them. That is very important in this business.
I am pleased that the federal Government is operating as a steward of our resources. At a time when we are to monitor financial institutions to make sure that they are solvent and functioning well, we can be facilitators to ensure that the industry on the West Coast can operate as it ought to. The opposition Parties are supporting us in this endeavour. I am pleased that they are, but I know that they are kind of reluctant debutantes. They would like to use this occasion to flail the Government. I am pleased they are supporting us because they know the welfare of western Canada is tied up in the welfare of a sound banking industry in British Columbia.
I return to my original statement. If the five major institutions had not been so avaricious in their dealings with Latin American countries, if they had not looked for an easy way out and over exposed themselves in Dome Petroleum, that $2 billion or $2.5 billion would have been available to Canadian consumers, particularly western Canadian consumers. They tried to negotiate a quick, slick deal with Dome Petroleum and leveraged themselves beyond all reason in the transaction. They withdrew from the small business community the millions and billions of dollars which would have been available to consumers and would have been of vital importance to the health of the business community, particularly in western Canada.
Again I return to my beginning remarks. This Bill will facilitate the operations of the Bank of B.C. so that it can
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
continue in business and can continue to contribute to a healthy western economy. In that event it will get its fair share of the market out there and provide healthy competition for the rest of the Canadian banking industry.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock- North Delta (Mr. Friesen). I listened to his speech. I would like the Member to explain to the House whether the difficulty of the Bank of British Columbia came from uncertainties facing depositors. In other words, were depositors withdrawing their funds because of lack of confidence in the bank after the unsuccessful bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank? Is it a question of confidence on the part of depositors or did the difficulty come from the quality of the assets? I would remind the Hon. Member that the Inspector General of Banks in October, 1985, after analysing the assets stated they were sound. Did the difficulty come from the deposit side of the balance sheet or from the value of the assets?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said in my earlier remarks, the man talks like a banker and he is good at reading ledgers. As I said to the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) the problem is solvency. When you are concerned about staying afloat, you are terribly concerned about why you are drowning. What you want is to be rescued. That is what we are dealing with today.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am very worried that government Members are reluctant to give us information. I do not disagree with the fact that the objective is to keep the regional banking system alive in western Canada. I said that in my speech yesterday, but it is the way it is done that concerns us. We are asking Canadians through CDIC to put $200 million into the equity of the Bank of Hongkong Canada, a division of the Bank of British Columbia which will be the Bank of Hongkong, without receiving any shares. The Bank of Hongkong will buy the quasi-totality of the assets and liabilities of the Bank of British Columbia for $62 million. If it is a question of uncertainties on the part of depositors, then the problem of the bank is a problem of liquidity, and there are solutions for that. If, however, the problem comes from the quality of the assets, that is another problem. Once again I want to ask the Member, who is a member of the government side and who must know the details, what is the situation about the quality of the assets? Another Member from British Columbia suggested yesterday that those assets may have to bear a $1.3 million loss. Is it true or not? I would like the Hon. Member to comment on that.

Madam
Speaker, unlike the previous speaker, I am saddened to stand up this Thursday, November 27 to rescue another failing bank. I think it is fair to say, without causing any undue concern, that we have been asked as a Parliament to rescue a failed bank.
We must be perfectly clear about what led up to this emergency debate in the House of Commons rescuing the Bank of British Columbia. I remember not many months ago when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the then Minister of State for Finance stood in their places and indicated that we had nothing to fear because the Inspector General of Banks had evaluated the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank in western Canada and said
November 27, 1986

they were totally sound and secure. The Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Bouey, spoke out publicly for one of the very first times in Canadian history and said Canadian depositors and people doing business with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank had nothing to fear, that everything was sound. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stood in his place and said we had nothing to fear, that everything was sound with the two western banks. As you well know, Madam Speaker, all of those people were wrong. The Governor of the Bank of Canada was wrong, the Inspector General of Banks was wrong, the Minister of Finance was wrong, the Minister of State for Finance was wrong, and the Prime Minister was wrong.
As a result of many, many months of inquiry into the collapse of these two western banks it turned out that there was a great deal of bungling going on. The Inspector General of Banks was pointed at and told that he did not do his job properly, and he has left his position, as he should have.
In a sense, and probably inadvertently, Members of the House of Commons and the Cabinet responsible for the Canadian banking industry misled Canadians. They were using, I guess, the best information presented to them by financial officials, the Inspector General of Banks and the Governor General of the Bank of Canada, and said everything was fine. The Inspector General of Banks, in October of 1985, sent an inspection team to review the Bank of British Columbia's loan portfolio. That review concluded that the portfolio was sound. It was a sound banking institution. All Members of Parliament from British Columbia knew for many, many months, as it was known on the streets of British Columbia and on the streets of the financial community in Canada, that that was not the case. Anyone who understands banking, anyone who understood what was going on in the British Columbia economy, knew that that was inaccurate. Yet once again we are being asked to co-operate with the Government to ensure that this rescue package is assembled in two days. Unfortunately, once again, our backs are against the wall. We have no choice but to co-operate and we do so in the best interests of the Canadian economy and financial community.
Whether they be borrowers, creditors, depositors or shareholders, the confidence western Canadians have in the ability of the Government to manage the financial affairs of Canada is abysmally low. The Government has bungled in the matter of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. When that happens, confidence is eroded. When word got out on the streets of western Canada that the Bank of British Columbia was in some difficulty, there was no confidence at all that the federal Government, the Inspector General of Banks, the Bank of Canada, or the Minister of Finance could do anything about it. In fact, I suspect a lot of people in western Canada were hoping that no one, not the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the Inspector General of Banks or anyone else would go to western Canada

If the Hongkong an Shanghai banking corporation wants to close down two-thirds of the Bank of British Columbia's branches, that is fine. If it wants to lay off all its employees in British Columbia, I guess that is okay. There are no guarantees. Nothing.
The Bank of British Columbia is a regional bank. It was set up so that western Canadians, mainly in Alberta and British

Columbia, could have their financial decisions made in western Canada. If you were putting a deal together you did not have to go to an eastern bank. People were suspicious of eastern banks. Yet we now have two easts here, the near east and the Far East. There was some fear of the near east. We said we do not want Toronto bankers. I certainly do not think British Columbians want Hong Kong bankers making investment decisions in the province. Yet that is exactly what we have. The major decisions on the what, where, when and how on investments will now be made in a foreign country. It was bad enough when they were being made in Toronto, but now they will be made in Hong Kong.
Do members of the Government really believe that a board of directors in Hong Kong will have the best interests of British Columbians at heart when it makes its financial decisions? Of course not. When the decisions were being made in Vancouver, the people involved were concerned about their friends, their communities and their industries. They were personally involved. That is the kind of financial institution we need in Canada. We need regional institutions in this country to cater to special needs.
We have sold out once again. This is a sell-out Government. There were other people interested. In the beginning there was a great deal of negotiation with Vancouver City Savings Credit Union, one of the largest credit unions anywhere. It is very profitable and sound and does an increasing level of business each year. It indicated an interest, but I suspect it got very little consideration from the federal Government or the British Columbia Government. Mr. Vander Zalm, the Premier of British Columbia, is delighted that a foreign bank now controls the Bank of British Columbia. I cannot see how anyone can be delighted that a British Columbia bank is now foreign controlled. I do not see how that is, to use his terms, "a fantastic idea".
The Vancouver City Savings Credit Union was a cooperative. I do not suspect it got much of a hearing when it put forth various options for taking over the Bank of British Columbia and continuing to operate it throughout the province. It needed support from the federal and provincial Governments which was not forthcoming. No one was prepared to entertain those ideas.
Let us be honest. I believe that both the federal Government and the provincial Government of British Columbia believe that foreigners can do the job better. It is almost as though we welcomed foreigners to take over when we get into difficulty. When the Continental Bank got in trouble, it was rescued by Lloyd's of London, a British bank. The Morguard Bank was taken over by Security Pacific Bank of Canada, which is a subsidiary of an American-based parent. Now the Bank of British Columbia is being taken over by the Hongkong Bank. I believe that the Government actually thinks this is good business, that it is in our best interest to lose control of our own destiny. New Democrats do not believe that.

That is not why the Bank of British Columbia was started. It was created to be sensitive to the needs and concerns of western investors, depositors and business people. It was concerned about its 1,400 employees. Now that this bank is in the hands of one of the largest foreign banks in the world, we have lost the sensitivity about which British Columbians felt so strongly that they kept their deposits in the bank during the very difficult times. I am disappointed that the Government did not make more of an effort to make a deal with a Canadian institution, specifically the Vancouver City Savings Credit Union which indicated a real interest. If it had been given the same support which the foreign bank received from the Government of Canada and a bit of support from the provincial Government of British Columbia, it could have put a deal together. We could have kept the decision-making on financial matters in British Columbia in the hands of British Columbians. Decisions on investment in B.C. could be made in board rooms in British Columbia rather than being subject to intervention from a foreign country.
If the Government of Canada had operated in a prudent, professional, business-like way in the best interests of western Canadians and had understood the reality of economic conditions in western Canada at the time, the Bank of British Columbia would not have gotten into difficulty. Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate today on the the sale of the assets of the Bank of British Columbia to the Hongkong Bank of Canada. I come to the debate with mixed feelings because, of course, as one who comes from British Columbia, I remember when the Bank of British Columbia originally started. I remember the very high hopes we had for it. We were all excited about having our own bank in British Columbia. Now because of what has happened in the last few years, we have come to the realization that the bank itself cannot stand on its own and that the assets must be sold. So in that sense it is not necessarily a happy debate.
On the other hand, I am very pleased that the Bank of British Columbia has been able to work out what I think will be an excellent purchase arrangement with the Hongkong Bank of Canada, and I would like to speak about some of these issues as we proceed in the debate.
I have been concerned by some of the comments I have heard from my colleagues opposite because I do not think they
truly reflect the situation with which we are dealing today. In fact, the legislation which is before us today is legislation which was asked for by the Board of Directors of the Bank of British Columbia. It is not something that the Government imposed on the bank. This is not a,Government deal about which we are talking. It is a private sector arrangement between the Bank of British Columbia and the Hongkong Bank of Canada.
In order for this arrangement to take place without further erosion of the assets or confidence in the Bank of British Columbia the legislation we are discussing today will enable the sale to go through and to delay a meeting with the shareholders for 14 days. As the Government what we are doing is helping to facilitate the arrangement. This is not in any way a sale that we have arranged ourselves.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), asked what the other options were. If we look back at what has happened over the last year in which the Bank of British Columbia recognized the difficulties it was facing, as my colleague from Saskatoon has mentioned, we see that many of these difficulties were brought on because of the previous Government's initiatives concerning an energy policy which left many western companies in a bad situation. As I remember it, the Bank of British Columbia had a great deal of sensitivity for western concerns and western companies. Unfortunately, many of the companies which have had loans with the bank have not succeeded and have fallen on hard times. The loss position in the bank's loan portfolio has increased dramatically. In fact, it was in the fourth quarter of this year that the bank recognized that with the growth in this loss position it would have to take action quickly or face liquidation.
I understand that in the last few months the bank has had discussions with a number of other financial institutions, including financial institutions in eastern Canada. Perhaps some Hon. Members will agree with the article in this morning's issue of The Globe and Mail which quotes the President of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, Mr. Robin Korthals. He is reported as saying that the deal with the Hongkong Bank of Canada was the best solution under the circumstances for the shareholders and depositors of the Bank of British Columbia. He stated that their only other alternative was liquidation. He also pointed out that despite overtures from the Bank of British Columbia to other major Canadian chartered banks, and some U.S.-based banks, eastern Canadian banks would be concerned about the problems in the Bank of British Columbia's loan portfolio.
I also know that there were discussions with Vancity and that some proposals were put forward. However, my understanding is that that company was not able to raise the capital required. Discussions then proceeded with the Hongkong Bank of Canada.
November 27, 1986

I would now like to clarify a point since there has been some discussion about the decisions being made offshore. What is happening with this transaction is that the assets of the Bank of British Columbia are being sold to the Hongkong Bank of Canada and the new bank will operate as a Canadian bank, a subsidiary of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank. The new bank will have its own board of directors based in Vancouver. Canadians will be involved in the decision making with regard to the future of the bank. It is not as if that function were suddenly to be shipped off someplace outside the country. The people I have met who will be involved with the bank have shown great concern and interest in the future of British Columbia. I have every confidence that they will make decisions that will be in the best interests of the business community and the depositors of British Columbia.
Another point I wish to make is that this sale is equivalent to 1 per cent of the total assets of banks in Canada. So in terms of foreign ownership it is a very minor portion of banking assets in Canada.
When one considers the alternatives compared to with what has happened, I must congratulate the Bank of British Columbia and the Hongkong Bank of Canada for being able to come to this arrangement. I believe it is an arrangement that will augur a great deal of potential in terms of the expansion of the bank's activities.
Premier Vander Zalm was here in Ottawa only yesterday. We met with him and he is pleased with this arrangement because it will give British Columbia another window into the Pacific Rim. We know of the extensive assets of the parent company, the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank. We know of its connections around the world and its experience and knowledge in terms of international finance. I believe it will be a positive asset in terms of opening up business opportunities in the Pacific Rim, something which is of top priority for British Columbia since we see much of our future in trade as being with the Pacific Rim.
One topic of discussion which we have undertaken with the Government is with respect to the possibility of establishing an international financial centre in Vancouver. The arrangement with the Hongkong Bank of Canada illustrates the importance of such a move, and it helps to facilitate its becoming a reality.
Other Hon. Members have mentioned a concern about what will happen to the branches and the employees. If a sale arrangement had been made with one of the traditional eastern banks which already has branches in British Columbia, then the chances would have been very great that the purchaser would close down the branches and that there would not be much potential for growth. However, the purchase by the Hongkong Bank of Canada, as pointed out by its President, presents an excellent opportunity for the Hongkong Bank to expand its personal branch network. Western Canada will continue to benefit by having a strong bank with its headquarters and its major assets in the west.

I recognize that there may have to be some rationalization in terms of the sale. We all know that in business people cannot be ordered to keep all their offices open and to keep all their employees. What the Hongkong Bank of Canada is buying as part of its assets is certainly these branches, deposits and goodwill that have been generated by the Bank of British Columbia. This deal augurs the best opportunity for the 1,400 employees and the 41 branches to be maintained.
There has also been some discussion that the taxpayers are involved in this deal. I would like to clarify that point because I think it is important that the public understand what is involved in this deal. The $200 million which the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will be putting into the new bank is money to help recapitalize it. The funds from the CDIC are not funds from the federal Government or from general revenues. They are funds that the CDIC collects on a premium basis from all banks in Canada. The payment of this sum of money will help to ensure the continued viability of the new Bank of British Columbia.
I think this is a much better deal for the depositors of the Bank of British Columbia and for British Columbians. The other alternative was liquidation. If the bank were liquidated, there would be nothing to pay out to the shareholders and there would have been a potential run of up to $1 billion on the CDIC as a result. It seems to me that this course of action is the prudent one in terms of being able to maintain the credibility of the deposit base and the employment in the bank for what I hope will be many years to come.
Because of the sale of the assets to the Hongkong Bank of Canada, we now look forward to the existence of a new bank in British Columbia. This bank will have the backing, expertise and network of the parent company and this will assure depositors. In my opinion, most of the employees and branches will be maintained. I would hope that the bank will be able to deal with the problems of outstanding loans and the loss provisions and once again emerge as a very healthy western-based bank, a bank that will indeed be sensitive to the kinds of initiatives and opportunities for expansion and trade in the Pacific Rim that we in British Columbia wish to undertake.
I think this initiative and many other initiatives the Government is now taking will improve the economic conditions in western Canada. I know that my colleagues on all sides of the House are familiar with those initiatives. There have been important initiatives in the energy industry. We have got rid of the National Energy Program and the PGRT. There has been $1 billion of assistance to western farmers and there are activities in British Columbia through ERDA agreements. The Micro-Tel agreement is helping to strengthen the business base in British Columbia.
In the past two days, a group of 50 business people from the secondary manufacturing sector in British Columbia came to Ottawa to seek out new opportunities. Many exciting businesses are starting out in British Columbia in the marine and

Member and the Government are prepared to break a bottle of champagne over this deal, but I think there are some tough questions to be asked. The question I am asking her is, can she stand in her place and agree that the funds from the employees' pension fund can be taken to sweeten the pay-off to the shareholders? I wish the Hon. Member would come clean with the House and tell the British Columbian people that is what she is prepared to do.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to reply to the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) on this question, because obviously it is a very important question. Perhaps I could draw his attention to the facts of what has actually happened with respect to the pension fund situation.
November 27, 1986

During the second quarter of the fiscal year 1986, the Superintendent of Insurance approved withdrawal of surplus contributions to the pension fund of the Bank of British Columbia, which was based on an independent actuarial report. That was then revoked and no further withdrawals were allowed, although it was left open for the Bank of British Columbia to reapply to withdraw the surplus, in accordance with new guidelines.
In connection with the sale to the Hongkong Bank of Canada, it is proposed that the pension plan accounts with the balances of all Bank of British Columbia employees be transferred to an equivalent pension plan with the Hongkong Bank of Canada. So those assets will be transferred. The Bank of British Columbia may reapply to the Superintendent of Insurance for permission to withdraw surplus funds remaining in the pension plan. If the application is successful, this surplus could accrue to the benefit of the shareholders. I would like to advise my hon. colleague that the Superintendent of Insurance and the Inspector General of Banks are on top of this situation. No withdrawals will be allowed if it is not in the interests of the employees of the pension fund. I can assure my colleague that they are much more aware than I am of how the actuarial benefits for the pension plan are done. I am confident that this matter will be addressed. If it is possible for any surplus funds to be transferred to the benefits of shareholders, it may be so. But there is no decision on that, and there will be no decision on that unless the Superintendent of Insurance and the head of the banking system for Canada are absolutely assured that that can be done without in any way harming the pension entitlement of the employees of the Bank of British Columbia. I am confident that this is the case.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot say I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate. However, I am doing so because my constituents in the riding of Ottawa-Vanier are starting to wonder about this Government's ability to manage its affairs. Considering the experience we had with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northlands Bank, we are very seriously wondering, first of all, whether the Government really wants to know what is going on, and second, whether it is a good manager. And I could argue demonstrably that the Government has been very remiss in the way it has managed the business of this country and has failed to give the House all the information it needs to be able to give all these issues careful scrutiny.
Madam Speaker, Bill C-27, an Act to facilitate the continuation of the business of the Bank of British Columbia, is one more example of the Government's incompetence and clearly shows that this Government has yet to establish an overall policy, to review legislation and keep its promises. Goodness knows, Madam Speaker, they said they would do so
Bank of British Columbia Business Continuation Act
many times. They said they would review all the legislation on financial institutions. And today we have yet to see any concrete evidence of this on the part of the Government.

I would like to remind the House that we have had at least seven or eight in-depth studies on the question of financial institutions, yet this Government has not come forth with anything. We had the Green Paper in April, 1985, we had the Wyman Report in June, 1985, we had the House of Commons committee go into the whole question in November, 1985, we had the Senate Finance Committee Report, we had the consultant's study on the Office of the Inspector General of Banks, we had the Estey Commission, and now we have from the Economic Council of Canada a whole document on this question published in November, 1986. Yet this Government has failed to act and has not come to terms with the problems that are facing this country. We are caught again in the House having to approve, in an adult manner, a very difficult situation. We are asked to approve urgently another bail-out of a bank.
Let me state very clearly that we are unfortunately in a situation of having to accept that information coming from the Government. We know for a fact, because of the documents that we have gathered overnight, that the information is not forthcoming, that the Government is not coming clean with us in the House as to what it knows on this matter. Therefore, we are very hesitant to go ahead and give the Government our support.
Nevertheless, will the Government make a reference of this whole question, in due course after passing the legislation, to the Finance Committee for extensive study? Will the Government allow witnesses, those involved in this whole mess, to come before the committee and explain to parliamentarians why this was necessary? We want to know when the Government will act on financial institutions. We want to have the assurance that the Government takes things seriously and will act accordingly. We would insist on guarantees for the staff of that bank. We would insist that they be taken into account and that the Government get the guarantees necessary for their continued employment. We would insist that the Government obtain from the Hongkong Bank an assurance that the Bank of British Columbia will be maintained as a regional bank. We believe that there is a need, and we believe that there is a right to have regional banks. We would like to see that guarantee from the Government that would give us that assurance. If we get these guarantees, reluctantly-very reluctantly-we will support this measure in the House.

Madam Speaker, the Government must act responsibly and, here again, it should take full responsibility for this disaster. The problems with the Bank of British Columbia are due to the incompetence of this Government and its lack of concern for the situation in our banks and for the need to amend the legislation on financial institutions. The Government has been

November 27, 1986
amateurish in this respect. We saw this with the Canadian Commercial Bank, we saw it with the Northland Bank, and we are seeing it again. They come rushing in with a piece of legislation and they tell Members: Take our word for it, adopt this Bill because it is vital to support this bank and prevent another bank from going bankrupt.

1 would like to give a brief summary, Madam Speaker, of what this Bill does. The Bill eliminates the need, under the Bank Act, for shareholders of a bank that has sold its assets to approve the transactions at a meeting to be held within 28 days of the announcement of the deal.
Second, the Bill proposes that 14 days' notice be given before calling a shareholders' meeting. Failure of the shareholders to adopt the proposal at the meeting will not affect the transaction itself. Instead, it would lead to the appointment of an assessor who will determine whether the $63.5 million paid by the Hongkong Bank should be increased or decreased. This evaluation would be binding. If the assessor concludes that the purchase price must be increased, CDIC, and not the Hongkong Bank, will pay the excess. If the assessor concludes that the purchase price must be decreased, the excess will be paid to the CDIC.
That is a brief summary, Madam Speaker, of this Bill. I will be brief because we are getting close to one o'clock. 1 would like to resume my comments at three o'clock.
This is a bail-out of a bank, Madam Speaker. It is a $200 million bail-out of a bank. Let us be frank about it. Let us call things as we see them, with the information that we have at our disposal right now and after reading the comments of the Minister and reading the comments of the Board of Directors of the BBC, which ruled out liquidation and I will quote as follows:
Liquidation is not a reasonable alternative, as realized asset values would-be affected to the point that it would be questionable whether any amount would be available for shareholders of BBC and there might well be a loss to uninsured depositors.

subtopic: ABORIGINAL RIGHTS
ABORIGINAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, important decisions are about to be announced by the Government on a new native claims policy. At last week's First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver, the government Leaders of both Yukon and the Northwest Territories tied the political and economic future of the North and its people to an acceptable new claims policy. They said that the new policy must recognize the right of aboriginal people to share in the resources of their traditional lands and to participate in the management and development of those resources.
On Monday Canadian churches sent a similar message to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), urging him to adopt a policy which recognizes aboriginal rights, including the right of self-government.
I expect these elements, which all fair-minded Canadians believe essential, must be incorporated into the new claims policy. I call upon the Government to announce the policy without any further delay.

subtopic: ALLEGED BREACH OF PHOTOCOPYING PRIVILEGES BY LIBERAL MEMBERS
ALLEGED BREACH OF PHOTOCOPYING PRIVILEGES BY LIBERAL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the media reported that several Liberal Members of Parliament who oppose a leadership review this weekend have used their House of Commons photocopying privileges to duplicate press clippings favourable to their present Leader.
One newspaper reported that a set of clippings containing 28 pages was mailed to 2,000 delegates. That is 56,000 photocopies for which Canadian taxpayers paid.
I suggest we review the "Unacceptable Requests" list from the House of Commons Printing Branch to see if this is acceptable.
Section 1 mentions that "solicitations of party membership" are a no-no, as are "requests for monetary contributions". Section 6 indicates that "party leadership election campaign material" is unacceptable according to the Printing Operation Branch.
I suggest that when the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) tells the media "if you want to have anything printed-you're more than welcome as a Member of Parliament, aren't you", the answer is no; 56,000 times no.
November 27, 1986

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO AMENDING PATENT LEGISLATION
OPPOSITION TO AMENDING PATENT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to share with the House some additional letters we have received from Canadians about the Government's proposal to amend the Patent Act in so far as pharmaceutical drugs are concerned. One writer writes:
Dear Mr. Broadbent:
I am very much opposed to any legislation put forward that would increase prices of drugs.
I have no medical plan for drugs and could not afford to buy them for my high blood pressure and arthritis, if they go any higher. I am not old enough to receive old age pension and there are many Canadians like me.
Another person writes to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) as follows:
I am 61 years old and have been retired for three years.
My wife and I live on a fixed pension which is not indexed as yours would be.
I enclose a photocopy of my most recent bill for Amiodorone. I am sure that you can readily verify my statement by contacting Toronto General Hospital... 1 can only wait very apprehensively to see what will happen to the prices of the rest of my medication.

P.S. And a very Merry Christmas to you too!

subtopic: SITUATION OF SUGAR-CANE REFINERIES
SITUATION OF SUGAR-CANE REFINERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concern has been expressed by sugar-cane refiners and those who use refined sugar in their products about the inquiry by the Canadian Tariff Board into the operations of Canadian sweeteners industries.
This sector is understandably afraid that measures will be installed to make raw sugar less competitive than it is now. Should this favourable situation be seriously disrupted, the consequences would be very serious indeed.
In Saint John, New Brunswick, there are 400 men and women employed at the Atlantic Sugar Refinery whose livelihoods depend upon the competitive price of raw sugar. There are many thousands more people throughout the city and the region whose livelihoods indirectly depend upon the vitality of the refinery. The refinery plays a significant role in the economy of the region. It brings business to the port and injects millions of dollars worth of business into various goods and services.
I would strongly urge that no action be undertaken which would disrupt the vitality and viability of sugar-cane refineries and force the loss of jobs in an area already suffering from high unemployment and a weak economic performance.

-I rise today to express my outrage at the attempt by the Government to raise the cost of prescription drugs for Canadians. Canadians are appalled that a Government elected on its commitment to protect sacred trusts would take such action that will undermine the health and well-being of Canadians.

subtopic: INCREASED PRODUCTION LEVELS-CREATION OF FAVOURABLE INVESTMENT CLIMATE
INCREASED PRODUCTION LEVELS-CREATION OF FAVOURABLE INVESTMENT CLIMATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Japan's most powerful business group has highly commended Canada as being one of the most promising markets for Japanese foreign investment.
Today I rise in praise of Canada's economic stability which has provided an incentive for countries such as Japan to invest with us. Canada has significantly improved production levels which are of the best among OECD industrial countries. Clearly the investment climate is favourable in Canada. Our energy costs are low and the labour force is well educated. Japan recognizes a strong relationship among academics, industry, and the Government in basic research and development, and the cost of production has become more competitive.

November 27, 1986

subtopic: LAY-OFFS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO INDUSTRIES
LAY-OFFS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a need for immediate action by the federal Government to halt the rapidly declining economy of northern Ontario. Week by week we hear of lay-offs, closings, and shutdowns of different forestry and mining operations which are the backbone of our northern economy, culminating yesterday in the announcement of the closure of northern Ontario's largest sawmill.
We all know that the Government is aware of the economic situation within the region for it has talked of what it calls a recovery package for northern Ontario. However, actions speak louder than policy papers, statements, and the establishment of even more committees. Time is of the essence and the people of northern Ontario are anxiously awaiting leadership on the lumber front, announcements that will result in actions leading to job creation and the end to recurring reports of the laying off of workers in Ear Falls, Sudbury, Terrace Bay, Nairn Centre, Wawa, Thunder Bay-and the list goes on and on.
Northern Ontario does not want patronage, palliatives, or a penitentiary, such as the one planned for the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding with the Solicitor General's (Mr. Kelleher) acquiescence. What our communities need are jobs.

subtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT ACTIONS
CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT ACTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is about four weeks ago today since we first learned that the Government and National Research Council senior officials were secretly arranging to close down the world-class Algonquin Radio Observatory in Algonquin Park. The Government is always bragging about promoting research and development, and yet it is destroying more science and technology and research and development in (Canada than it ever thought of implementing.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and every Tory candidate talked about the wondrous things that were going to happen in the science [ community and every area of the Canadian economy. Today
Canadians are wondering how they are ever going to tolerate or withstand another two and a half years of this Government. Everything the Government puts its hands on, from science and technology to the softwood lumber industry, seems to disintegrate before our very eyes.
The phasing out of the observatory in Algonquin Park and the severe cuts in science and technology are a disgrace on the part of the Government, and the departure of highly trained Canadians to other countries to find new challenges is a brain drain on Canada from which it will take many years to recover. It will be three weeks tomorrow since the announcement by British Telecommunications to close down the four year-old Mitel plant in the town of Renfrew-

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-REPRESSION OF RELIGIOUS FREEDOM
U.S.S.R.-REPRESSION OF RELIGIOUS FREEDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a Canadian it is impossible to imagine being the object of harassment or imprisonment for religious beliefs. It is a scenario we cannot comprehend because religious freedom is considered a basic human right to which we are entitled as Canadian residents. For Pavlo Hryhorovych Protsenko, a Ukrainian religious dissident, such freedom must seem luxury indeed. On June 4 of this year he was arrested while visiting the home of a nun. His family has been subjected to threats of arrest for attempting to defend his position. Prior to his arrest, Protsenko was detained at a Moscow station and searched, ostensibly, for drugs. All that was found was a Bible, a prayer book, a cross, and a religious manuscript describing the life of orthodox believers in the U.S.S.R. Dangerous items indeed.
It is inconceivable that we who enjoy such freedoms should stand silently by while such acts of repression are perpetrated against those who dare to stand up for their religious beliefs. I urge the Government to make Soviet officials forcefully aware of our opposition to their continued repression of religious freedom.

subtopic: PARTISAN ADVERTISING
PARTISAN ADVERTISING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that, this fall, Quebecers received correspondence from the office of the leader of the socialist Party.
November 27, 1986

This overtly political message relates to old age security pensions and the Canadian tax system, it is printed on House of Commons stationery, and it was delivered by Canada Post at taxpayers' expense.
Can the socialist leader explain why his Party did not pay for distributing their partisan literature?
Should the majority of Canadians, who are not socialists, be expected to foot the bill for this socialist message?
The socialist leader often talks about fairness, justice and integrity, but he ought to be the first one to show respect for Canadian taxpayers by paying for his own publicity without reaching into the pockets of others.

subtopic: PROPORTION OF WOMEN IN JOB TRAINING PROGRAMS
PROPORTION OF WOMEN IN JOB TRAINING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women released a very important study on the status of women in education, training, and development. The study says the proportion of women in federal job training programs dropped 10 per cent between 1977 and 1985. Those were Liberal years. Since the National Training Act came into effect in 1979, women's participation has dropped every year.
The federal Government dumped the NTA and replaced it with programs under the Canadian Jobs Strategy. CJS emphasizes private-sector training. The Congress believes that emphasis will worsen the trend of participation by women because employers are more likely to train men than women. As executive director Aisla Thompson observed: "CJS puts the training money into employers' hands ... you can reach your own conclusion". This important study says that setting targets for groups such as women is not good enough. The Congress calls for controls which will monitor the amount and type of training women receive.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR AMENDING PATENT LEGISLATION
SUPPORT FOR AMENDING PATENT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, drug prices will not go up as a result of Bill C-22. Yesterday four prominent Canadian medical researchers strongly endorsed our Government's plan to provide patent protection to producers of newly-discovered drugs. They, as well as other academics, including Dr. John Bachinsky, Dean of Pharmacy at the University of Alberta, agree that these changes are long overdue.
Dr. Jacques Gagne, Dean of Pharmacy at the University of Montreal, used the example of a powerful new heart drug called milrinone. That drug is unavailable here as the manufacturer does not want to leave it open to copy-catting by generic drug producers. As you can see, Canadians are missing out on the latest drug discoveries. Why should we be forced to do without the best in medical technology? Why should we allow a brain drain to the U.S.? As a pharmacist and concerned Canadian, I, too, add my voice to the strong support given these changes and urge all Canadians to endorse the fairness of full patent protection for the benefit of all Canadians.

subtopic: CN SHOPS IN MONCTON-GOVERNMENT POSITION
CN SHOPS IN MONCTON-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day in New Brunswick, people heard the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) say on the radio that CN should buy rails from SYSCO and create jobs for workers in Cape Breton.
I certainly agree with the Minister that CN should try and create jobs for Canadians. Only yesterday, CN announced it will be laying off 87 workers in Moncton, adding up to a total of 403 since 1985.
Why do we never hear federal Ministers from New Brunswick support local workers? We never hear them say that CN should maintain its shops in Moncton.
Why shouldn't these Ministers do like their colleague, the Minister of National Revenue? Why the silence about the CN shops?
If the problem is ever settled, the Ministers will never be able to say they did what they could, because they did nothing. If 1 didn't know better, I would think that as far as the CN shops are concerned, New Brunswick has no representation at all in Cabinet.

JAPANESE REPORT ON FAVOURABLE INVESTMENT CLIMATE IN CANADA

subtopic: STATEMENT MADE BY CANADIAN MINISTER

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the process of irradiating certain foods, such as in the treatment of potatoes, onions, wheat, and flour, has been used in the United States for some period of time. I have recommended that we put forward proposed new regulations regarding the process, possibly in February next year. There is then a period in which there can be public comment. That did not exist before when regulations were to be changed. It is the process we now have in mind. Every study by the United Nations, agriculture, and the World Health Organization, within their prescribed limits, indicates that it is a safe process.

Mr. Speaker, again I remind the House that the Official Opposition reluctantly agreed to the Government request to study and adopt Bill C-27 in one and a half days. Mr. Speaker, we did so because we were concerned about employment security and also because of our strong support for this regional concept. We want to say quite clearly that even though we feel compelled to believe this Government, it will have to bear the onus of proof, assume its responsibilities, and produce all figures and details for the Canadian public, because it was the Government that brought this issue before the House and sought our support. We are prepared to co-operate, but we can tell the Government that we have just about had it, we are beginning to be rather tired because, ever since this Parliament opened, we have been asked many times to rescue this Government which does not know how to manage, behaves like an amateur, and shows incompetence when it has to deal with such important issues as our financial institutions. Mr. Speaker, I am not mincing my words because this same Government has delivered two throne speeches in which it kept repeating that it would introduce a Bill to eliminate the flaws in the legislation on financial institutions.
I do not want to take too much time. I know the House wants to proceed to the question and we would like to get into Committee of the Whole. However, I want to give a brief overview of this Bill. It is indeed a bail-out, a $200 million bail-out, by CDIC. We are operating in a policy vacuum. The Government has failed to come forward with legislation to tighten control over financial institutions. Over the last year we have been asked, after the fact, to legislate the Imasco-Genstar takeover, the Lloyds Bank merger, and here we are again being asked to approve this takeover after the fact. The Government promised on many occasions, in every Throne Speech and every speech made on the CCB and Northland Banks, that everything would be all right. The Government asked us to trust it. However, everything was not all right. The Government had not done its homework. It did not know what it was talking about. We trusted the Government but we are
November 27, 1986

getting pretty fed up with doing that when it does not deserve it.

I hear them laughing over there. This is not a laughing matter. We are talking about billions of dollars. We are talking about the financial institutions which are so very important to the survival of this country, economically and otherwise.
I want to touch on two very specific items. First, the CD1C will have to put up $200 million, and in return the Hongkong Bank will buy the B.C. Bank for $63.5 million. Shareholders will have no say. According to the Bill, if they do not agree with the deal an assessor will be named. The assessor will decide whether the purchase price of $63.5 million is all right. If it is excessive, the excess will go back to the shareholders of CDIC. If it is deficient, then the CDIC will have to produce the money to allow the deal to go through.
Then there is the question of the pension fund. I know the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) is not here but she mentioned that this morning. I agree with her to a certain extent that the BBC received permission from the Superintendent of Insurance to withdraw the pension fund surplus. That surplus could go back to the shareholders if, and this is the big "if', the Superintendent of Insurance allows it. Our position is that since the CDIC is the one doing the bail-out, it should get that money. Even better, the employees, whose pension fund is at stake here, should get the money.
We are concerned about the jobs involved and the regional bank system. We are concerned about this whole deal. We will be asking questions in Committee of the Whole. We will support the Bill in principle. We have to because the Government says it has an obligation to govern and we will help it to do so. However, we are getting pretty damn fed up with giving this Government our confidence.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext: Madam Chairman, effectively, there seems to be in this deal the fact that the Government of Canada will give $200 million to the Hongkong Bank in order to facilitate its taking over the assets of the Bank of British Columbia, with a payment of some smaller sum to shareholders. Is this payment related to a reluctance on the part of the Government to see a credit union grow the way that Vancouver City Savings Credit Union would have grown had it gone ahead with the projected merger which was under very active discussion just a couple of weeks ago and which was suddenly forgotten at the time the Hongkong Bank deal came forward?

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I think this is one of the more important issues which can be raised with regard to the Bill. I am happy to respond to the Hon. Member. Since we are limited in time and there may be a number of questions with regard to the Bill, I will try to answer as many questions as possible as quickly as possible.
With respect to the question of Vancity, it was afforded the same degree of consultation and opportunity to bid as anyone else. It turned out at some point in time that there was an agreement between Vancity and the Bank of British Columbia to begin negotiations. There was no agreement on the deal, but there was an agreement to begin negotiations, which did not go anywhere. With respect to what actually happened, the Hon. Member will have to ask those involved in the transaction. Of course, all we are doing here with the Bill is facilitating a sale and dealing with the time period concerning the notification of shareholders.
I have been told that the parties could not consummate a deal because Vancity's capital base was not sufficient to go it alone. It was something like a mouse swallowing an elephant. If Vancity could have obtained a large source of capital to add to its own capital base then it might have been able to go through with the transaction. However, that did not happen and then this other offer emerged.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I would like to pursue this matter a bit further. The Minister knows that the Vancity proposal included a request to which the Province of British Columbia was sympathetic, that is, that it participate thereby enabling the Bank of British Columbia or its successor to remain as an important and regionally-controlled financial institution which would operate under the control of British Columbia in the Province of British Columbia.
We have often seen situations of foreign bidders being given contracts in Canada because they have the technology while Canadian companies with equivalent skills are shunted aside or ignored because they are seen to be too small or inexperienced. These companies cannot get the experience because they cannot get the bids and therefore they cannot grow. It seems to me that this may be the case in this particular instance as well.
Did the Government indicate to Vancity that if the B.C. Government was prepared to come into the deal, it would have the political will to put this deal through, or was the Government's indication of being willing to legislate, as we are now, only a commitment made to the Hongkong Bank? In other words, were we kowtowing to a foreign bank because of its size while failing to co-operate with a domestic institution on the grounds that it was too small?

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, it was not the Government that was involved in these discussions, it was the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was aware of the discussions because it
November 27, 1986

might have been asked to participate at some point in arrangements leading to a deal.
I think the Hon. Member would have to ask the Government of British Columbia about what went on between Vancity and the Government of British Columbia. The assessment made by the Government of British Columbia in deciding whether or not to help in this transaction would be something about which the Hon. Member should ask that Government. Otherwise, I would have to make the same inquiry myself. Since this was a private transaction, I think it would be best for the Hon. Member to ask the Government of British Columbia what its assessment of that was.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, in the first place, government consent was required for the transfer of assets. Therefore, the Government cannot say that it was not involved. Presumably, if the Bank was seeking the Government's consent, some discussions were taking place.
Second, is the Minister saying that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation committed $200 million to this deal without the approval of the Government or was the approval of the Government sought? I find it inconceivable that the CDIC would make this commitment without informing and getting the approval and acceptance of the Government.

subtopic: BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA BUSINESS CONTINUATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I understand the question. The Government was not informed in the first instance of any Vancity-Bank of British Columbia discussions because a deal had not been put together which involved the CDIC. It never got to the stage that the Government would have to be informed. We were informed, of course, of the arrangement which is the background to the Bill we are putting forward now.
The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation made some prudential decisions. It decided that a capital provision of $200 million for the Hongkong Bank of Canada would do two things. First, it would protect the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation against the future because this new entity, a strong bank almost the size of the world Bank of Canada, would be taking the bank over with its reputation and resources behind it. All the uninsured depositors and liabilities would be off the hands of the CDIC and would be taken on by this new entity. Therefore, protection against the future was part of the reason for the expenditure of $200 million.
The second reason is that the money is to be used as a source of capital, as a provision against future loan losses and as a capital base that will allow the Bank to do any corporate reorganizations that may be required. The decision made by the CDIC protects against the future and provides capital for a strong base for the present. CDIC decided that $200 million was much better than what it would have been exposed to had there been a liquidation. It could have been exposed to an amount many times greater than that.

I have in my possession a press release by the Bank of British Columbia which perhaps will provide the Hon. Member with some additional information. In terms of suitors or how long the courting period went on, I think it really started in the summer. The Bank of British Columbia was becoming increasingly concerned about non-performing loans and loan-loss provisions. There were not many suitors, I must say from what I understand, but there were a few. The Hongkong Bank emerged in the fall as a serious suitor. However, I would not say that in the summer it was necessarily involved as a serious suitor, although I think the name was mentioned.
The whole canvas was initiated as a matter of prudent foresight really as early as late 1985, according to the press release, when the Board of Directors of BBC concluded that BBC like a number of other smaller Canadian banks would have difficulty recovering from the loss of confidence which followed events then taking place in the banking system and that the time for recovery might be unacceptably long. Then the canvas was accelerated during recent weeks when it became apparent that the BBC financial results for the fourth quarter ending October 31 could signal a worsening of the financial position of BBC. "This would be likely to continue through 1987 and probably longer", to quote from the press release. Tentative discussions were initiated during this recent period with a number of possible candidates.
I am glad to talk about the press releases of various parties to the transaction. However, essentially what we are doing in the Bill is just facilitating a private arrangement by adjusting the time period of notice for shareholders.

Madam Chairman, in answer to the Hon. Member's first question I will again refer to the press release. It indicates that expeditious completion of the transaction was essential if the continuity of the business of BBC was to be
November 27, 1986

preserved and the interests of depositors, employees, shareholders, and others were to be protected. In recognition of this, the BBC has requested the Government of Canada to introduce before Parliament special legislation to authorize expeditious completion of the transaction. That is what we are doing now.
In terms of the worst case scenario, I do not know how helpful it is to portray a nightmare scenario. However, I will give the Hon. Member the facts. If the Board of Directors of the Bank of British Columbia feels, as it felt, that the possibility of the bank remaining viable in the months ahead is very slender, we are faced with $1.3 billion worth of deposits insured by CDIC. That is a very big hit on the CDIC's budget, less whatever is recuperated by way of assets. That is the worst case scenario. That is the liquidation. Depositors would be nervous and would go somewhere else. As British Columbians they would probably have to go to a non-regional institution. Borrowers would be very unsettled and this experiment of having a regional bank would have failed.
A very important thing about this deal is that not only are the depositors doing business as usual, and borrowers doing business as usual with the regional bank continuing to go from strength to strength with a very good capital base, it will have an international network which is really what the people of British Columbia have been looking to in terms of trade, investment and everything else. It is something we have had some difficulty putting in place up until now.

Madam Chairman, some people are trying to shirk their responsibilities and wash their hands of the whole affair.
Madam Chairman, we have eight minutes left till 4:30 p.m., when the Minister, as agreed, will go to the other place to answer questions from Members of the other half of this parliamentary institution to which we belong.
For the first time, a Minister, the Minister of State for Finance, is saying and repeating, as a Minister of this

Government, that the possible loss on the transaction could be around $1.3 billion.
